articles.title: Federal Constitutional Court moved for ban on social media use by kids under 16
articles.description: LAHORE: A petition has been filed before the Federal Constitutional Court (FCC), seeking directions to shield children under 16 from unrestricted social media use and indecent content on television and other platforms. Two lawyers, Sheraz Zaka and Moin Akhtar, filed the petition at the Lahore registry, with the former identifying himself as an activist and the latter as the father of a minor child. The petitioners argue that Pakistani children are being exposed to cyber bullying, addictive platform design, sexualised content and the glorification of alcohol — all of which they say harm children’s mental and moral development. They claim that no Pakistani law currently mandates age verification for social media access, noting that the Prevention of Electronic Crimes Act (Peca), 2016, contains no specific restriction for users under 16. Citing examples of Australia, Italy, and Brazil as countries that have already imposed under-16 social media bans , the petitioners argue that such regulation is both feasible and necessary. Plea claims no law mandates age verification for social media access They allege that the Pemra failed to enforce its own code of conduct, allowing dramas and advertisements containing intimate scenes and alcohol depictions to air during hours when children are likely watching. The petitioners also refer to Pakistan’s broader education crisis, citing figures that roughly 25 million children in the country are out of school — reportedly the highest number of out-of-school children anywhere in the world. The petitioners assert that the government’s failure to act violates articles 9, 14, 25, 25-A and 35 of the Constitution, which guard the rights to life, dignity, equality, education and family protection. They also invoke the Convention on the Rights of the Child and a prior Lahore High Court ruling (PLD 2020 Lahore 137) that directed the state to legislate on human rights and social issues. The lawyers ask the FFC to direct the federal government to amend Peca 2016 to restrict social media access for under-16s with an age-verification mechanism, and and order to the Pemra to strictly enforce content standards during child-viewing hours. They also seek a direction to the government for coordination with social media platforms on parental controls and action on out-of-school children and dropout rates. The petitioners describe it as the first such petition filed in the country on the issue. The federal government through the ministry of law and justice, the ministry of information technology, the National Cyber Crime Investigation Agency, the Pemra and the Pakistan Telecommunication Authority have been listed as respondents in the petition. Published in Dawn, September 9th, 2026

articles.title: Sindh Assembly demands Centre abolish petroleum levy
articles.description: KARACHI: The Sindh Assembly on Tuesday unanimously adopted an opposition resolution demanding that the Centre abolish petroleum levy tax. As Jamaat-i-Islami (JI) is staging sit-ins across the country against rising prices of petroleum products, its lone lawmaker in the house, Muhammad Farooq, moved the resolution demanding the abolition of the petroleum levy tax. Responding to the resolution, Law and Parliamentary Affairs Minister Ziaul Hasan Lanjar said that the matter pertained to the federal government and the provincial government could not abolish the tax. Later, the speaker put the resolution for vote and the house unanimously adopted it, urging the federal government to end the levy tax. House unanimously adopts JI lawmaker’s resolution against rising fuel prices; MQM-P stages noisy protest against ‘Sindhudesh’ The JI member’s resolution said that at present, the actual price of petrol including customs duty was Rs238.70, but in addition to this price, the government was charging Rs80 as petroleum levy, Rs5 as climate levy, and Rs25.3 per litre as margin of oil marketing companies. “Through these additional levies, not only petrol and diesel have become more expensive, but inflation has also increased proportionately. This has placed 95 per cent of the people of Pakistan under the burden of inflation, which amounts to severe oppression of the public,” it said. “Therefore, through this resolution, this House demands that the federal government immediately end the government levy and other duties and provide immediate relief to the public,” the resolution said. Muttahida protests against ‘Sindhudesh’ Earlier, proceedings were marred as opposition lawmakers belonging to the Muttahida Qaumi Movement-Pakistan staged a noisy protest against the so-called Sindhudesh, preventing Question Hour from being held during the Private Members’ Day sitting. The assembly session, chaired by Speaker Syed Awais Shah, was disrupted within minutes when MQM-P’s Deputy Parliamentary Party Leader Taha Ahmed rose to address the house on the issue of “Sindhudesh” during Question Hour. Moments later the house echoed with loud protests and sloganeering as opposition members disrupted the proceeding, forcing the speaker to intervene repeatedly. The chair asked the protesting lawmakers to take their seats and let the Question Hour continue. “The entire house is watching, the entire Sindh is watching,” he remarked as opposition members continued their protest. The MQM-P lawmakers converged in front of the speaker’s rostrum and chanted “Sindhu Desh na manzoor, Speaker gardi na manzoor”. The ruckus began after Leader of the Opposition Ali Khurshidi of the MQM-P accused treasury members of running video clips of assembly proceedings on their social media accounts. He alleged that even ministers were involved in the practice. “We consider you impartial,” Mr Khurshidi told the chair, referring to an earlier incident where an apology was sought from an opposition member for recording video in the house. The speaker responded: “Alright, give me the list.” During Question Hour, Taha Ahmed kept speaking while the MQM-P members did not ask supplementary questions. Later, speaking to reporters at the Media Corner on the premises of the Sindh Assembly, Opposition Leader Khurshidi condemned what he called the “partisan attitude” of MQM-P members did not ask supplementary questions. Later, speaking to reporters at the Media Corner on the premises of the Sindh Assembly, Opposition Leader Khurshidi condemned what he called the “partisan attitude” of the speaker and the assembly secretariat. “Constitutionally, Private Members’ Day belongs to the opposition. Until now we considered the speaker to be impartial, which is why we supported him. But after being reprimanded by the chief minister, he has become biased,” he alleged. Christian Family Law bill introduced Deputy Speaker Anthony Naveed also introduced the Christian Family Laws Bill 2026 in the house. “It has been 150 years and Christian family law has come to the assembly. I request the opposition to support it. My wish is that the bill be introduced and referred to the committee today,” he said. The bill was referred to the relevant standing committee. Published in Dawn, September 9th, 2026

articles.title: Flock Employee Calls Cops on Reporter Filming Them
articles.description: Flock Safety wants to record millions of Americans—but apparently no one is allowed to record them. The disturbing double standard was revealed Tuesday by Atlanta News First , which found itself in a load of trouble after one of its investigative reporters stopped on the side of the road to film a Flock Safety employee upgrading one of the company’s cameras near his house. Brendan Keefe—a Peabody-, duPont-, Murrow-, and Emmy-winning journalist—pulled ahead of the Flock Safety site in a marked press van, donned a high-visibility vest, and began snapping pictures. Almost immediately, the Flock Safety employee chucked his equipment into his truck and fled the site. Keefe tried to tail the vehicle, but his efforts were interrupted by the Milton Police Department, who sent out three police vehicles after the Flock employee summoned them. “I work with Flock Safety and I’m getting followed, harassed, pretty much, taking video and pictures,” the employee said in a 9-1-1 call obtained by the local news network. When the operator prompted the employee to provide his name, he opted not to, claiming that he didn’t “want them to hear my full name” on the call “when they get it.” Taking pictures and videos in public spaces, where there is no reasonable expectation of privacy, is protected under the First Amendment. But Flock Safety’s close relationship with police departments across the country seems to have afforded the company protections beyond the scope of the Constitution. “When you are lawfully present in a public space—such as streets, sidewalks, and parks—the First Amendment generally protects your right to photograph or film anything in plain view, including federal buildings and law enforcement,” according to the American Civil Liberties Union . Flock Safety deployed its first mass surveillance camera (which was, at the time, an Android phone placed inside a waterproof box) in Atlanta in 2017. Since then, the company has deployed tens of thousands of cameras to record and document the movements of everyday Americans, regardless of whether or not they’re suspected of a crime. That data is then sold to law enforcement agencies, offering them a seemingly infinite porthole into the potentially consequential habits of their countrymen. In April, the company—and its business model—were valued at $8.4 billion. In most cases, the cameras were installed without community consent. The company has repeatedly defended its product, claiming that the cameras have provided more safety , and that the cited abuses stem from the way that police use their data, rather than the collective of the data itself. “Ultimately, I would argue that the whole community is our customer,” Flock Safety Chief Communications Officer Josh Thomas told Atlanta News First. “Why can’t I opt out? Why can’t the spouse or ex-spouse of a police officer opt out of this kind of data collection on their movements?” asked Keefe. “Why can’t a person opt out?” repeated Thomas. “It’s because if your car gets stolen, if something were to happen, moreover the government requires you to have a license plate.” “It’s plain viewing information,” Thomas continued, missing the bitter irony of the situation. “Why can’t you opt out? You can, if you want to opt out of society.”

articles.title: Youth clubs, trade unions, pubs: here's how Burnham can fix Britain's social recession | Gordon Brown
articles.description: From volunteering to the WI, we have lost so many ways to meet our neighbours. Making that easier can only be good for society Prime minister Andy Burnham has hit the ground running, tackling head-on three of the public’s burning concerns: falling standards of living, failing public services and a remote, out-of-touch, over-centralised Whitehall. Now, this autumn, a fourth challenge, reversing the decades-long decline of civic engagement, is about to move centre stage to achieve his ambition to put citizens back in control of their communities. For while there are tens of thousands of local champions bringing towns, cities and villages together, Britain is suffering a civic recession, a hollowing out of the associations, clubs and organisations that once were the beating hearts of our communities. Gordon Brown was UK prime minister from 2007 to 2010 Continue reading...

articles.title: ‘It was very hurtful’: darts cult hero Stephen Bunting on death threats, social media – and the new Luke Littlers
articles.description: The world No 10 on getting recognised in New York, coping with hostility and why he’s never changing his walk-on song “Definitely,” Stephen Bunting says as he considers whether working so hard as a darts player on social media is like making a deal with the devil. After Luke Littler, the prodigiously gifted teenage world champion , Bunting is the most heavily marketed player in darts. But, over the past year, some of his success on and off the oche has been accompanied by vicious abuse. Bunting has had death threats and he recently moved his eldest son to a private school to end the bullying which had hounded 14‐year‐old Toby, who often shares his social media space. But Bunting remains amiable and happy to reflect on his Faustian pact during a lucrative rollercoaster ride through darts. Continue reading...
